The limits matter: central multiple events keep their existing fixed floor, and this method does not yet give polynomial cost jointly in height and accuracy bits.

I’ll read the r3 packet and check the previous history capture, then work through whether pure-P query costs can depend on binary height while retaining the full physical tuple and root/filter costs.

The route now has two cases. If the regulator terms are small enough on the retained integration region, I can bound their omission error and evaluate simpler logarithmic formulas. Otherwise, the requested precision is already large enough to pay for the existing method. I’m checking this across the full weak tuple, including the heat residual and density mass.

The provider calculation also avoids evaluating the exponentially small carrier itself: it uses arm logarithms, normalized ratios, and argument reduction for the large phase. The proposed bound therefore depends on requested bits and binary height for certified pure-P queries. It leaves the global source-construction cost separate.

The same-model checks found no blocking gap in r3’s saturation, integration, or provider costs. I’m tightening the constant choices and recording the result: polynomial query cost in requested bits and binary height, with global source construction charged separately.

The proof now covers both precision regimes: at large heights, a paid saturation bound removes the expensive weight scale; when requested precision is high enough to prevent that shortcut, the remaining height cost is already polynomial in the bit budget. I’m saving the note and assessment, then preparing r4’s all-height cost ledger. No numerical research runs were performed.
